title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning

paper.title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context.
As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated ‘forget set’ without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities.
Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model p θ p_{\theta} to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence KL ( p θ ∥ p anchor ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\bigr) .
We identify two failure modes of MDU.
First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked.
Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence KL ( p anchor ∥ p θ ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta}\bigr) logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget.
Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses,
we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked.
On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) trained on web-scale corpora inevitably memorize sensitive personal information, copyrighted material, and private facts. Machine unlearning ( Cao & Yang, 2015 ; Bourtoule et al., 2021 ) addresses the urgent need to remove designated training data from a deployed model so that forget-set information can no longer be elicited, while preserving performance on retain data. While unlearning in autoregressive (AR) models has matured via gradient ascent ( Jang et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , preference optimization ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , and bounded and reweighted objectives ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , with dedicated benchmarks ( Maini et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) and unified evaluation suites ( Dorna et al., 2025 ) , extending these concepts to alternative generative paradigms presents distinct challenges. In particular, AR unlearning objectives operate on a single, well-defined next-token log-likelihood, whereas MDLMs train and generate over randomly masked positions and timesteps with no fixed unmasking order; porting such an objective therefore means choosing how to mask and sample for it, a choice that can leave forgotten content recoverable through masking patterns the objective was never defined over. While concept erasure in continuous image diffusion models ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ) has demonstrated the feasibility of altering denoising trajectories, generative unlearning for discrete text diffusion remains under-explored. The emergence of Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) —such as LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) —presents a fundamental shift in text generation. By iteratively denoising sequences of masked tokens via bidirectional context rather than left-to-right prediction, MDLMs achieve strong generative performance and global sequence coherence. As these architectures scale to frontier capabilities ( Bie et al., 2025 ; Inception Labs et al., 2025 ) , ensuring safety and unlearning becomes critical. Recently, Lee et al. (2026) introduced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU), the first publicly available unlearning framework tailored for MDLMs. It aligns the model’s output on a forget set , p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{t}) , with a prompt-masked unconditional anchor, p anchor ( ⋅ ∣ ∅ , y t ) p_{\mathrm{anchor}}(\cdot\mid\emptyset,y_{t}) , scaled by a temperature hyperparameter τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau\in[0,1] , via the anchor-last divergence KL ( p θ ∥ p anchor ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\bigr) . This term is combined with a standard cross-entropy loss on a retain set when available. However, we identify two critical limitations of MDU, which we will elaborate on in this paper: (i) Knowledge leakage: Anchor-last KL pulls p θ p_{\theta} toward the diffuse masked anchor by matching the model’s aggregate output distribution rather than directly suppressing the probability of ‘forget tokens’, so sensitive tokens remain recoverable within the resulting noisy generation trajectories even at the anchor’s most diffuse setting (Figure 1 ); moreover, under random partial masking, unmasked answer tokens can remain visible to the anchor’s own null-context forward pass, so its “unconditional” prediction may still concentrate on the sensitive part of the answer ; and (ii) Vanishing ‘forget gradient’: at a memorized (near-one-hot) masked-token prediction, the anchor-last KL’s gradient vanishes while the anchor-first KL’s gradient does not; as a result, under finite-step training (and due to practical nonconvexity, even non-finite), MDU learning stalls exactly on the tokens we most need to forget. We ask whether the choice of divergence direction, not just the anchor (as suggested in Lee et al. (2026) ), is the primary lever for forgetting quality in MDLMs. A second, orthogonal design choice is how the anchor is constructed: under random partial masking, unmasked answer tokens can remain visible to the null-context model, so the unconditional prediction may still concentrate on the forget answer; masking the entire answer span removes that cue. We propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning ( EMDU ), which replaces the anchor-last objective with the anchor-first divergence KL ( p anchor ∥ p θ ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta}\bigr) and fully masks target answer spans when forming the anchor. Empirically, the unlearned model typically abstains on forget queries by emitting empty (EOS-only) completions rather than fluent paraphrases of the sensitive fact. An empty completion is a safer output mode for unlearning: emitting no tokens is auditable and cannot itself leak partial or hallucinated forget-set content, whereas a long incoherent answer can still include leaks (see MDU generations with τ = 0 \tau=0 in Figure 1 ) and a fluent paraphrase risks either regurgitating the original fact or confidently asserting a plausible-sounding wrong one, which is harder to detect and arguably worse for a downstream user, especially in critical applications (see MDU generations with τ = 1 \tau=1 in Figure 2 ). Our key Contributions: • We introduce EMDU , a new unlearning method that combines anchor-first KL with full answer-span masking, achieving stronger forgetting and superior retain-set utility over MDU, as well as over prominent methods adapted from AR LLMs to MDLM, on TOFU and RWKU benchmarks with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B. • We theoretically establish that the anchor-last gradient vanishes on memorized forget tokens (and can be small also in a large area around them, making it hard to escape them) while the anchor-first gradient does not. We support this limitation with experiments on real data. • We will open-source our project and release (upon acceptance): the models after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on TOFU (no such models are currently available), EMDU checkpoints for LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on TOFU and RWKU, and full evaluation scripts.

sections.heading: 2.1 Machine Unlearning
sections.text: Problem formulation. Given a model M M pre-trained on 𝒟 = 𝒟 f ∪ 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{f}\cup\mathcal{D}_{r} , where 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} denotes the forget set (e.g., sensitive personal data or copyrighted text) and 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} the retain set , machine unlearning produces an updated checkpoint M ∗ M^{*} satisfying two competing objectives: (i) forgetting : M ∗ M^{*} should no longer reveal information from 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} ; and (ii) retention : M ∗ M^{*} should preserve model performance on 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} and standard downstream tasks. Unlearning methods. Early approaches established gradient ascent (GA) on 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} as a baseline ( Jang et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , though unconstrained GA causes catastrophic collapse on general capability. Subsequent work addresses stability: Gradient Difference (GD) ( Maini et al., 2024 ) balances GA on 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} with gradient descent on 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} ; Negative Preference Optimization (NPO) ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) and SimNPO ( Fan et al., 2025 ) reframe forgetting as bounded preference optimization; Weighted Gradient Ascent (WGA) ( Wang et al., 2025 ) applies token-level weighting to limit collapse; and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) is adapted into an unlearning baseline that prefers a refusal ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) or a perturbed answer over the forget response. Dedicated benchmarks such as TOFU ( Maini et al., 2024 ) , RWKU ( Jin et al., 2024 ) , WMDP ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and MUSE ( Shi et al., 2025 ) probe different unlearning settings, and unified evaluation suites such as OpenUnlearning ( Dorna et al., 2025 ) standardize methods and metrics across them. All of the above methods were originally designed for autoregressive LLMs. As mentioned above, recently, Lee et al. (2026) introduced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU), the first publicly available unlearning method designed for MDLMs, which we describe in detail in § 2.3 . Unlearning in image diffusion models. A parallel line of work targets concept erasure in continuous image diffusion models (e.g., ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , AdvUnlearn ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) ). These methods optimize continuous noise trajectories to alter visual outputs. Because they rely on Gaussian noise schedules over continuous latents, they do not directly transfer to the discrete absorbing-state masking process of text-based MDLMs. Adversarial robustness. Concurrent work by Zhang et al. (2026) (made publicly available after MDU ( Lee et al., 2026 ) ) finds that unlearning performance in MDLMs is sensitive to generation length and denoising steps. It proposes adversarial RL, in which a separate LLM generates contexts that elicit forgotten knowledge while the MDLM learns, via GRPO, to suppress it.

sections.heading: 2.2 Masked Diffusion Language Models
sections.text: Continuous image diffusion has become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity image generation, editing, and restoration ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021a ; Song et al., 2021b ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Garber & Tirer, 2024 ; Garber & Tirer, 2025 ) , modeling data as iterative denoising of corrupted inputs. Masked Diffusion Language Models inherit this conceptual foundation for discrete text. Discrete diffusion was formalized by D3PM ( Austin et al., 2021 ) using absorbing-state transitions, and refined by SEDD ( Lou et al., 2024 ) via score-entropy matching. MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) simplified this into a substitution-based framework (their SUBS parameterization, which enforces zero probability of predicting [ 𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺 ] [\mathtt{MASK}] and carries over already-unmasked tokens unchanged) , showing that the continuous-time ELBO reduces to a weighted sum of cross-entropy terms over masked positions. Block Diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) extends this framework block-wise, interpolating between diffusion and autoregressive generation. Scaled backbones LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) extend MDLM’s architecture to multi-billion-parameter instruction models. LLaDA trains a bidirectional Transformer from scratch; Dream initializes from an AR checkpoint to leverage pre-trained LLMs. Both adopt the following standard MDLM corrupting process. Consider the vocabulary 𝒱 = { 1 , … , V } \mathcal{V}=\{1,\ldots,V\} . At timepoint t ∼ U ( 0 , 1 ] t\sim U(0,1] , each response token y ( i ) y^{(i)} (word from the vocabulary) is independently masked with probability t t , yielding noisy sequence y t y_{t} with masked-position set ℳ t = { i ∣ y t ( i ) = [ 𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺 ] } \mathcal{M}_{t}=\{i\mid y_{t}^{(i)}=[\mathtt{MASK}]\} . The model p θ ​ ( y ( i ) ∣ x , y t ) p_{\theta}(y^{(i)}\mid x,y_{t}) uses full bidirectional context to reconstruct masked tokens. We present the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) form of this ELBO, where the prompt x x is held fixed and only the response y y is masked (unlike pretraining, which masks the entire sequence with no prompt held out). This SFT objective essentially has the following cross-entropy loss form, used throughout this paper for the base SFT and for the retain term: ℒ CE ( x , y , t ; θ ) = − 1 t ∑ i ∈ ℳ t log p θ ( y ( i ) ∣ x , y t ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(x,y,t;\theta)\;=\;-\frac{1}{t}\sum\nolimits_{i\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}\log p_{\theta}(y^{(i)}\mid x,y_{t}), (1) where 1 / t 1/t , the ELBO weight under this linear schedule, reweights token positions according to masking density. Lastly, note that the same model can be run conditionally on a prompt x x , written p θ ( ⋅ | x , y t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{t}) , or unconditionally by replacing the prompt with masks ∅ \emptyset , written p θ ( ⋅ | ∅ , y t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot|\emptyset,y_{t}) . This is the discrete analogue of classifier-free guidance’s split ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , where the model supports both conditional and unconditional denoising.

sections.text: MDU. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning training objective tailored for MDLMs ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . The model being optimized is computed by the conditional denoiser: p θ = p θ ( ⋅ | x , y t ) p_{\theta}=p_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{t}) . Both are compared only at the masked answer positions ℳ t = { i ∣ y t ( i ) = [ 𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺 ] } \mathcal{M}_{t}=\{i\mid y_{t}^{(i)}=[\mathtt{MASK}]\} (as in Eq. ( 1 )): the forget KL is applied only at i ∈ ℳ t i\in\mathcal{M}_{t} , averaged uniformly over | ℳ t | |\mathcal{M}_{t}| . KL orientation. We write anchor-last for KL ( p θ ∥ p anchor ) \mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\mathrm{anchor}}) and anchor-first for KL ( p anchor ∥ p θ ) \mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\|p_{\theta}) . MDU calls the anchor-last direction “forward KL”—the opposite of the widespread convention in variational inference and knowledge distillation, where “forward” usually denotes KL ( target ∥ model ) \mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{target}\|\mathrm{model}) ( Minka, 2005 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . We use anchor-last / anchor-first throughout to keep the argument order unambiguous. MDU minimizes the anchor-last divergence: ℒ AL ( x , y , t ; θ ) = KL ( p θ ∥ p anchor ) = ∑ k = 1 V p θ , k log p θ , k p anchor , k . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}(x,y,t;\theta)\;=\;\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}})\;=\;\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{V}p_{\theta,k}\log\frac{p_{\theta,k}}{p_{\mathrm{anchor},k}}. (2) This is a per-token quantity, computed at each masked answer position i ∈ ℳ t i\in\mathcal{M}_{t} and averaged uniformly over | ℳ t | |\mathcal{M}_{t}| . Setting τ = 0 \tau=0 collapses p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} to a uniform distribution (maximum-entropy noise); τ = 1 \tau=1 matches unconditional model predictions. MDU quantifies this continuum with LLaDA pseudo-perplexity on TOFU (Table 7 in their paper): forget PPL is extremely high at low τ \tau and falls toward base as τ \tau increases, while retain/RA/WF PPL stay near the base model. Figure 1 further shows that low- τ \tau generations can still surface forget tokens despite being incoherent, and Figure 2 shows that at τ = 1 \tau{=}1 generations become fluent but can be confidently wrong or leak the correct answer. To preserve utility, MDU combines this forget objective, 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ 𝒟 f , t ​ [ ℒ AL ​ ( x , y , t , θ ) ] \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{f},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}(x,y,t;\theta)] , with a standard cross-entropy retain loss, 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ 𝒟 r , t ​ [ ℒ CE ​ ( x , y , t , θ ) ] \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{r},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(x,y,t;\theta)] , computed on 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} and weighted by a scalar α \alpha . Under the usual variational inference notation, where p p is fixed and q q is optimized, KL ( p ∥ q ) \mathrm{KL}(p\|q) (anchor-first) is described as mass-covering and KL ( q ∥ p ) \mathrm{KL}(q\|p) (anchor-last) as mode-seeking ( Minka, 2005 ) . This heuristic rests on p , q p,q being continuous, unimodal densities fit from samples, and is known not to transfer cleanly to LLM knowledge distillation, where the fitted distributions are instead discrete, high-dimensional categorical distributions ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, both orientations are strictly convex in q q and share the same unique minimizer q = p q=p ( Cover & Thomas, 2006 ) , so mode-seeking/mass-covering cannot explain why anchor-first outperforms anchor-last in practice, as will be shown in this paper. We argue that the reason is dynamical: § 4 shows that for a near-one-hot SFT initialization on a forget set’s token, anchor-last’s gradient vanishes early in training while anchor-first’s gradient does not. This is exacerbated by practical nonconvexity: in practice, more iterations do not resolve this limitation.

sections.heading: 3 EMDU: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
sections.text: In this section, we propose our Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU) method. EMDU keeps MDU’s frozen prompt-masked anchor and temperature τ \tau and changes two ingredients: the forget divergence, and how the anchor’s answer span is corrupted. § 4 analyzes the divergence; this section specifies the procedure. Empirically, the resulting model often abstains on forget queries by emitting empty (EOS-only) completions which, as discussed in § 1 , is a safe unlearning output.

sections.heading: 3.1 Anchor-first forget loss
sections.text: Let p θ p_{\theta} be the optimized model at a masked response position and p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} the frozen prompt-masked anchor, as in § 2.3 . MDU minimizes the anchor-last KL, EMDU instead minimizes the anchor-first KL: ℒ AF ( x , y , t ; θ ) = KL ( p anchor ∥ p θ ) = ∑ k = 1 V p anchor , k log p anchor , k p θ , k . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}(x,y,t;\theta)\;=\;\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta})\;=\;\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{V}p_{\mathrm{anchor},k}\log\frac{p_{\mathrm{anchor},k}}{p_{\theta,k}}. (3) This uses the same ℳ t \mathcal{M}_{t} masking and uniform averaging as MDU’s forget loss (Equation ( 2 )). Gradient dynamics of the two KL directions are compared in § 4 , showing that anchor-first KL better fits unlearning from confidently memorized (near-one-hot) predictions .

sections.heading: 3.2 Full answer-span masking
sections.text: Under MDU, the optimized model and frozen anchor share the same randomly masked answer y t y_{t} , where each token is masked independently with probability t t . The optimized model is conditioned on the prompt ( x , y t ) (x,y_{t}) ; the anchor is evaluated on the prompt-masked pair ( ∅ , y t ) (\emptyset,y_{t}) . Unmasked forget tokens therefore remain as bidirectional context for the frozen model. The KL is applied only on masked positions—there is no loss on the visible ones in y t y_{t} —but those survivors shape p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} at the masked slots (since y t y_{t} is inputted to p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} ) . Therefore, the target that the optimized model is pulled toward can still concentrate on the forget answer. Figure 3 illustrates the failure: a few surviving answer tokens can cue the sensitive span in the anchor’s masked-position predictions. EMDU thus applies full answer-span masking (FAM) on the anchor forward only : every answer position is replaced by [ 𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺 ] [\mathtt{MASK}] when forming p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} , while the optimized model continues to see randomly masked y t y_{t} . FAM changes the anchor input, and does not affect the computation of p θ p_{\theta} . sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: TOFU setup and metrics. We fine-tune LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct on TOFU ( Maini et al., 2024 ) full to obtain Base SFT checkpoints, using the fine-tuning hyperparameters suggested by MDU (Appendix D.2 ), then unlearn on forget10 with retain90. All training and evaluation runs use NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. Unless otherwise noted, TOFU generations use 128 128 denoising steps and 128 128 output tokens (the MDLM answer canvas), matching the MDU evaluation protocol. Following MDU, we report Rouge-L recall (rL) and answer probability ( p p ) on Forget, Retain, Real Authors (RA), and World Facts (WF). Rouge-L (rL) is Rouge-L recall between the generated string and the reference answer. Answer probability p p is defined in Appendix D.1 . RWKU setup and metrics. We consider the first 10 subjects (out of 200 subjects total) of the RWKU ( Jin et al., 2024 ) dataset, the same subset used by MDU. We match MDU’s metrics: F-L1/N-L1 (knowledge memorization), F-L2/N-L2 (knowledge manipulation via paraphrased/reasoning QA), and F-L3 (robustness to adversarial-attack prompts)—all Rouge-L recall, following RWKU’s official protocol—plus MMLU, TruQA, and TriQA. Unlike TOFU, RWKU does not require fine-tuning: we unlearn each subject independently from the off-the-shelf Instruct checkpoint, using that subject’s official RWKU forget pairs ( 582 582 prompt–response biographies per entity) and no retain set. Base rows are macro averages over those ten subjects (mean of per-subject means for forget and neighbor; TruQA / TriQA likewise over ten subjects; MMLU is the shared utility suite). Examined Methods. We compare to the same baselines from Lee et al. (2026) adapted from AR to MDLM: GA, GD, NPO, SimNPO, WGA, DPO with the addition of MDU, each tuned over learning rate and training length (Appendix D ). GD is not relevant for RWKU, which does not have a designated retain set. For MDU and EMDU, we set τ = 1 \tau=1 . In Appendix F (Figure 7 ) we sweep τ \tau for both methods and show that: 1) our EMDU with τ = 1 \tau=1 outperforms MDU with any τ \tau examined, and 2) our EMDU is usually stable with respect to τ \tau .

sections.heading: 5.2 Robustness
sections.text: Generation robustness . The concurrent work of Zhang et al. (2026) shows that unlearning effectiveness for diffusion language models is highly sensitive to generation hyperparameters, particularly output length and the number of denoising steps. We therefore re-evaluate checkpoints across all six output-length/denoising-step combinations they use ; full numbers are in Table 7 (Appendix F ). EMDU keeps near-zero Forget across this range on both backbones , with Retain / RA / WF declining only mildly , on the order of the SFT baseline’s own sensitivity . MDU is markedly less stable under coarser sampling . Paraphrased questions. Empty forget completions on the original phrasing do not by themselves show that the fact is gone: a model could still answer a reworded probe. We therefore also evaluate forget10 with TOFU’s official paraphrased questions: Table 8 (Appendix F ) shows EMDU’s Forget stays near zero under paraphrase on both backbones, while SFT remains high, so EMDU’s forgetting does not depend on the exact question wording. Seed variance. The methods in Tables 3 and 4 are trained and evaluated at a single fixed seed, following the practice of Lee et al. (2026) , due to limited compute resources. We re-run EMDU’s chosen configurations for TOFU and RWKU with 2 2 additional independent unlearning seeds per backbone and report mean ± \pm std in Tables 9 and 10 (Appendix F ). The resulting spread is small across both datasets and both backbones, and EMDU’s Forget and Retain remain clearly separated from MDU’s single-seed numbers in Table 3 in every seed we ran, showing that its advantage over MDU is not an artifact of the particular seed reported.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusions
sections.text: We presented EMDU : anchor-first KL with full answer-span masking for unlearning in masked diffusion language models. On TOFU, the method strongly reduces the forget-set’s Rouge-L and answer probability while preserving retain and probe utility, and typically abstains with EOS-only canvases on forget queries. Relative to MDU, abstention avoids the gibberish-vs-fluency tradeoff along τ \tau , and the empty canvas can be rendered as a fixed or templated response at deployment time . Future research can explore whether the same gradient-saturation mechanism identified in § 4 also explains KL-direction choices in other settings built on the same divergence, such as knowledge distillation and post-training ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: E.1 MDU reproducibility
sections.text: We were unable to reproduce Lee et al. (2026) ’s reported numbers from released artifacts alone; this subsection documents what we found while attempting to.

sections.heading: Checkpoints.
sections.text: The official repository releases neither the Base SFT checkpoint used before unlearning nor any unlearned (post-MDU) checkpoint, for either backbone; the SFT code itself is likewise not part of the release, and the checkpoint it would have produced must be supplied externally to run the unlearning script.

sections.heading: Unlearning hyperparameters.
sections.text: Their Implementation Details section reports only the training setup shared across all methods—AdamW, a cosine learning-rate schedule, gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 , batch size 4 4 (effective 16 16 with accumulation 4 4 on TOFU)—and gives a concrete learning rate and epoch count for Base SFT ( 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , 1000 1000 / 300 300 epochs for LLaDA / Dream) but no learning-rate value or epoch/step count for the unlearning stage itself, for MDU or for any baseline.

sections.heading: TOFU forget/retain sampling.
sections.text: Their training script tokenizes the forget and retain splits separately, merges them into a single dataset, and shuffles the result; a training row is therefore either a forget example or a retain example, drawn independently, rather than a forget example and a retain example evaluated together at every step. This differs from TOFU’s own reference implementation and from OpenUnlearning, where the forget-retain training dataset returns one forget example and one (randomly sampled) retain example together at every index, so both terms are seen at every step. Moreover, their released configuration’s retain path defaults to retain_perturbed.json rather than retain90.json : retain_perturbed is an evaluation-only split of TOFU (its paraphrased and perturbed answers feed the retain-side metrics reported across their evaluation suite), not a training retain set, so using it as the retain regularizer risks overfitting toward the evaluation distribution itself. We patch this default to retain90 whenever we run their code.

sections.heading: Rouge-L: F1 vs. recall.
sections.text: Their paper defines Rouge-L as an F1 (longest-common-subsequence F-measure) metric, but their released evaluation scripts for both TOFU (LLaDA and Dream) and RWKU (Dream) all compute scorer.score(gt, pred)["rougeL"].recall , i.e. Rouge-L recall , not F1. Recall (not F1) is also what TOFU’s own official evaluation code reports (its eval_rouge_recall function). It is therefore unclear whether the Rouge-L numbers in their paper were produced by this released code (recall) or by a different, unreleased computation matching their stated F1 definition.

sections.heading: RWKU forget corpus.
sections.text: Their RWKU conversion scripts reference per-target-model generated forget-pair files (distinct file paths for a LLaDA-generated and a Dream-generated version of the corpus), consistent with RWKU’s protocol of generating the forget corpus with the target model itself; neither this generated data nor the scripts used to produce it are included in the release. We instead use RWKU’s publicly released Llama-generated forget corpus for both backbones (§ E ), so that our RWKU numbers do not depend on unreleased, model-specific data. Their release is also asymmetric across backbones on the evaluation side: it includes an RWKU evaluation script for Dream ( eval_rwku_dream.py ) but none for LLaDA, despite shipping a LLaDA-targeted RWKU conversion script ( convert_rwku_to_tofu.py ).

sections.heading: RWKU MMLU prompt.
sections.text: Their released RWKU evaluation ( eval_rwku_dream.py ) scores MMLU by generating a few tokens and taking the first character of the output as the predicted choice, with the few-shot prompt’s closing “ Answer: ” cue placed at the end of the user message, before the chat template is applied. RWKU’s official evaluation ( eval_mmlu.py ) instead appends “ Answer: ” after the assistant header, so the model’s reply begins directly with the choice. The placement matters little for Dream, which answers with a bare letter under either prompt (off-the-shelf Dream-7B-Instruct: 0.740 0.740 with their placement, 0.760 0.760 with RWKU’s). LLaDA, however, often restates the cue (“Answer: C”), which the first-character rule reads as “A”: off-the-shelf LLaDA-8B-Instruct scores 0.400 0.400 with their placement and 0.680 0.680 with RWKU’s. Their paper reports 0.395 0.395 for this model, close to the first value; since the release contains no LLaDA RWKU evaluation script, we cannot tell how that number was obtained. All MMLU numbers in Table 4 use RWKU’s placement with the same first-character rule.

sections.heading: Appendix G Qualitative Examples
sections.text: This appendix illustrates the abstention behavior quantified in § 5.1 ( Empty completions ): EMDU typically returns an empty completion on forget queries, whereas the baselines answer and can reveal the forgotten fact. Figures 8 – 9 show this on RWKU and TOFU. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated ‘forget set’ without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model p θ p_{\theta} to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence KL ( p θ ∥ p anchor ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\bigr) . We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence KL ( p anchor ∥ p θ ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta}\bigr) logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) trained on web-scale corpora inevitably memorize sensitive personal information, copyrighted material, and private facts. Machine unlearning ( Cao & Yang, 2015 ; Bourtoule et al., 2021 ) addresses the urgent need to remove designated training data from a deployed model so that forget-set information can no longer be elicited, while preserving performance on retain data. While unlearning in autoregressive (AR) models has matured via gradient ascent ( Jang et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , preference optimization ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , and bounded and reweighted objectives ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , with dedicated benchmarks ( Maini et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) and unified evaluation suites ( Dorna et al., 2025 ) , extending these concepts to alternative generative paradigms presents distinct challenges. In particular, AR unlearning objectives operate on a single, well-defined next-token log-likelihood, whereas MDLMs train and generate over randomly masked positions and timesteps with no fixed unmasking order; porting such an objective therefore means choosing how to mask and sample for it, a choice that can leave forgotten content recoverable through masking patterns the objective was never defined over. While concept erasure in continuous image diffusion models ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ) has demonstrated the feasibility of altering denoising trajectories, generative unlearning for discrete text diffusion remains under-explored. The emergence of Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) —such as LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) —presents a fundamental shift in text generation. By iteratively denoising sequences of masked tokens via bidirectional context rather than left-to-right prediction, MDLMs achieve strong generative performance and global sequence coherence. As these architectures scale to frontier capabilities ( Bie et al., 2025 ; Inception Labs et al., 2025 ) , ensuring safety and unlearning becomes critical. Recently, Lee et al. (2026) introduced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU), the first publicly available unlearning framework tailored for MDLMs. It aligns the model’s output on a forget set , p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{t}) , with a prompt-masked unconditional anchor, p anchor ( ⋅ ∣ ∅ , y t ) p_{\mathrm{anchor}}(\cdot\mid\emptyset,y_{t}) , scaled by a temperature hyperparameter τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau\in[0,1] , via the anchor-last divergence KL ( p θ ∥ p anchor ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\bigr) . This term is combined with a standard cross-entropy loss on a retain set when available. However, we identify two critical limitations of MDU, which we will elaborate on in this paper: (i) Knowledge leakage: Anchor-last KL pulls p θ p_{\theta} toward the diffuse masked anchor by matching the model’s aggregate output distribution rather than directly suppressing the probability of ‘forget tokens’, so sensitive tokens remain recoverable within the resulting noisy generation trajectories even at the anchor’s most diffuse setting (Figure 1 ); moreover, under random partial masking, unmasked answer tokens can remain visible to the anchor’s own null-context forward pass, so its “unconditional” prediction may still concentrate on the sensitive part of the answer ; and (ii) Vanishing ‘forget gradient’: at a memorized (near-one-hot) masked-token prediction, the anchor-last KL’s gradient vanishes while the anchor-first KL’s gradient does not; as a result, under finite-step training (and due to practical nonconvexity, even non-finite), MDU learning stalls exactly on the tokens we most need to forget. We ask whether the choice of divergence direction, not just the anchor (as suggested in Lee et al. (2026) ), is the primary lever for forgetting quality in MDLMs. A second, orthogonal design choice is how the anchor is constructed: under random partial masking, unmasked answer tokens can remain visible to the null-context model, so the unconditional prediction may still concentrate on the forget answer; masking the entire answer span removes that cue. We propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning ( EMDU ), which replaces the anchor-last objective with the anchor-first divergence KL ( p anchor ∥ p θ ) \mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta}\bigr) and fully masks target answer spans when forming the anchor. Empirically, the unlearned model typically abstains on forget queries by emitting empty (EOS-only) completions rather than fluent paraphrases of the sensitive fact. An empty completion is a safer output mode for unlearning: emitting no tokens is auditable and cannot itself leak partial or hallucinated forget-set content, whereas a long incoherent answer can still include leaks (see MDU generations with τ = 0 \tau=0 in Figure 1 ) and a fluent paraphrase risks either regurgitating the original fact or confidently asserting a plausible-sounding wrong one, which is harder to detect and arguably worse for a downstream user, especially in critical applications (see MDU generations with τ = 1 \tau=1 in Figure 2 ). Our key Contributions: • We introduce EMDU , a new unlearning method that combines anchor-first KL with full answer-span masking, achieving stronger forgetting and superior retain-set utility over MDU, as well as over prominent methods adapted from AR LLMs to MDLM, on TOFU and RWKU benchmarks with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B. • We theoretically establish that the anchor-last gradient vanishes on memorized forget tokens (and can be small also in a large area around them, making it hard to escape them) while the anchor-first gradient does not. We support this limitation with experiments on real data. • We will open-source our project and release (upon acceptance): the models after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on TOFU (no such models are currently available), EMDU checkpoints for LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on TOFU and RWKU, and full evaluation scripts. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Machine Unlearning Problem formulation. Given a model M M pre-trained on 𝒟 = 𝒟 f ∪ 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{f}\cup\mathcal{D}_{r} , where 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} denotes the forget set (e.g., sensitive personal data or copyrighted text) and 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} the retain set , machine unlearning produces an updated checkpoint M ∗ M^{*} satisfying two competing objectives: (i) forgetting : M ∗ M^{*} should no longer reveal information from 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} ; and (ii) retention : M ∗ M^{*} should preserve model performance on 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} and standard downstream tasks. Unlearning methods. Early approaches established gradient ascent (GA) on 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} as a baseline ( Jang et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , though unconstrained GA causes catastrophic collapse on general capability. Subsequent work addresses stability: Gradient Difference (GD) ( Maini et al., 2024 ) balances GA on 𝒟 f \mathcal{D}_{f} with gradient descent on 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} ; Negative Preference Optimization (NPO) ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) and SimNPO ( Fan et al., 2025 ) reframe forgetting as bounded preference optimization; Weighted Gradient Ascent (WGA) ( Wang et al., 2025 ) applies token-level weighting to limit collapse; and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) is adapted into an unlearning baseline that prefers a refusal ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) or a perturbed answer over the forget response. Dedicated benchmarks such as TOFU ( Maini et al., 2024 ) , RWKU ( Jin et al., 2024 ) , WMDP ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and MUSE ( Shi et al., 2025 ) probe different unlearning settings, and unified evaluation suites such as OpenUnlearning ( Dorna et al., 2025 ) standardize methods and metrics across them. All of the above methods were originally designed for autoregressive LLMs. As mentioned above, recently, Lee et al. (2026) introduced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU), the first publicly available unlearning method designed for MDLMs, which we describe in detail in § 2.3 . Unlearning in image diffusion models. A parallel line of work targets concept erasure in continuous image diffusion models (e.g., ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , AdvUnlearn ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) ). These methods optimize continuous noise trajectories to alter visual outputs. Because they rely on Gaussian noise schedules over continuous latents, they do not directly transfer to the discrete absorbing-state masking process of text-based MDLMs. Adversarial robustness. Concurrent work by Zhang et al. (2026) (made publicly available after MDU ( Lee et al., 2026 ) ) finds that unlearning performance in MDLMs is sensitive to generation length and denoising steps. It proposes adversarial RL, in which a separate LLM generates contexts that elicit forgotten knowledge while the MDLM learns, via GRPO, to suppress it. 2.2 Masked Diffusion Language Models Continuous image diffusion has become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity image generation, editing, and restoration ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021a ; Song et al., 2021b ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Garber & Tirer, 2024 ; Garber & Tirer, 2025 ) , modeling data as iterative denoising of corrupted inputs. Masked Diffusion Language Models inherit this conceptual foundation for discrete text. Discrete diffusion was formalized by D3PM ( Austin et al., 2021 ) using absorbing-state transitions, and refined by SEDD ( Lou et al., 2024 ) via score-entropy matching. MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) simplified this into a substitution-based framework (their SUBS parameterization, which enforces zero probability of predicting [ 𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺 ] [\mathtt{MASK}] and carries over already-unmasked tokens unchanged) , showing that the continuous-time ELBO reduces to a weighted sum of cross-entropy terms over masked positions. Block Diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) extends this framework block-wise, interpolating between diffusion and autoregressive generation. Scaled backbones LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) extend MDLM’s architecture to multi-billion-parameter instruction models. LLaDA trains a bidirectional Transformer from scratch; Dream initializes from an AR checkpoint to leverage pre-trained LLMs. Both adopt the following standard MDLM corrupting process. Consider the vocabulary 𝒱 = { 1 , … , V } \mathcal{V}=\{1,\ldots,V\} . At timepoint t ∼ U ( 0 , 1 ] t\sim U(0,1] , each response token y ( i ) y^{(i)} (word from the vocabulary) is independently masked with probability t t , yielding noisy sequence y t y_{t} with masked-position set ℳ t = { i ∣ y t ( i ) = [ 𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺 ] } \mathcal{M}_{t}=\{i\mid y_{t}^{(i)}=[\mathtt{MASK}]\} . We present the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) form of this ELBO, where the prompt x x is held fixed and only the response y y is masked (unlike pretraining, which masks the entire sequence with no prompt held out). This SFT objective essentially has the following cross-entropy loss form, used throughout this paper for the base SFT and for the retain term: ℒ CE ( x , y , t ; θ ) = − 1 t ∑ i ∈ ℳ t log p θ ( y ( i ) ∣ x , y t ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(x,y,t;\theta)\;=\;-\frac{1}{t}\sum\nolimits_{i\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}\log p_{\theta}(y^{(i)}\mid x,y_{t}), (1) where 1 / t 1/t , the ELBO weight under this linear schedule, reweights token positions according to masking density. This is the discrete analogue of classifier-free guidance’s split ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , where the model supports both conditional and unconditional denoising. 2.3 Unlearning for Masked Diffusion Models MDU. We write anchor-last for KL ( p θ ∥ p anchor ) \mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\mathrm{anchor}}) and anchor-first for KL ( p anchor ∥ p θ ) \mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\|p_{\theta}) . MDU calls the anchor-last direction “forward KL”—the opposite of the widespread convention in variational inference and knowledge distillation, where “forward” usually denotes KL ( target ∥ model ) \mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{target}\|\mathrm{model}) ( Minka, 2005 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . (2) This is a per-token quantity, computed at each masked answer position i ∈ ℳ t i\in\mathcal{M}_{t} and averaged uniformly over | ℳ t | |\mathcal{M}_{t}| . Setting τ = 0 \tau=0 collapses p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} to a uniform distribution (maximum-entropy noise); τ = 1 \tau=1 matches unconditional model predictions. MDU quantifies this continuum with LLaDA pseudo-perplexity on TOFU (Table 7 in their paper): forget PPL is extremely high at low τ \tau and falls toward base as τ \tau increases, while retain/RA/WF PPL stay near the base model. Figure 1 further shows that low- τ \tau generations can still surface forget tokens despite being incoherent, and Figure 2 shows that at τ = 1 \tau{=}1 generations become fluent but can be confidently wrong or leak the correct answer. To preserve utility, MDU combines this forget objective, 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ 𝒟 f , t ​ [ ℒ AL ​ ( x , y , t , θ ) ] \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{f},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}(x,y,t;\theta)] , with a standard cross-entropy retain loss, 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ 𝒟 r , t ​ [ ℒ CE ​ ( x , y , t , θ ) ] \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{r},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(x,y,t;\theta)] , computed on 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{r} and weighted by a scalar α \alpha . Under the usual variational inference notation, where p p is fixed and q q is optimized, KL ( p ∥ q ) \mathrm{KL}(p\|q) (anchor-first) is described as mass-covering and KL ( q ∥ p ) \mathrm{KL}(q\|p) (anchor-last) as mode-seeking ( Minka, 2005 ) . This heuristic rests on p , q p,q being continuous, unimodal densities fit from samples, and is known not to transfer cleanly to LLM knowledge distillation, where the fitted distributions are instead discrete, high-dimensional categorical distributions ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, both orientations are strictly convex in q q and share the same unique minimizer q = p q=p ( Cover & Thomas, 2006 ) , so mode-seeking/mass-covering cannot explain why anchor-first outperforms anchor-last in practice, as will be shown in this paper. We argue that the reason is dynamical: § 4 shows that for a near-one-hot SFT initialization on a forget set’s token, anchor-last’s gradient vanishes early in training while anchor-first’s gradient does not. This is exacerbated by practical nonconvexity: in practice, more iterations do not resolve this limitation. 3 EMDU: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning In this section, we propose our Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU) method. EMDU keeps MDU’s frozen prompt-masked anchor and temperature τ \tau and changes two ingredients: the forget divergence, and how the anchor’s answer span is corrupted. § 4 analyzes the divergence; this section specifies the procedure. Empirically, the resulting model often abstains on forget queries by emitting empty (EOS-only) completions which, as discussed in § 1 , is a safe unlearning output. 3.1 Anchor-first forget loss Let p θ p_{\theta} be the optimized model at a masked response position and p anchor p_{\mathrm{anchor}} the frozen prompt-masked anchor, as in § 2.3 .
